newsitem.title: UK: UK DROPS PLANS TO SHIFT BURDEN OF PROOF ON MERGERS.
newsitem.headline: UK DROPS PLANS TO SHIFT BURDEN OF PROOF ON MERGERS.

text.p: The British government has dropped plans to require companies seeking control of others via mergers to show the deals are in the public interest, a statement on Thursday by Trade and Industry Secretary Margaret Beckett showed.
Writing in the foreword to a draft government bill which would revise competition law, Beckett said she saw "no need to change the burden of proof" in merger cases.

The new law, expected to be introduced into parliament in the autumn, proposes, as expected, the creation of a new Competition Commission to take over the functions of the Monopolies and Mergers Commission and to hear appeals against decisions of the Director-General of Fair Trading.

At the May general election, Labour campaigned on a platform of, as its policy handbook described it, "shifting the onus of proof in cases where the proposed merger has been referred to the competition authorities".
The party said it would "require the company seeking control to demonstrate that it would be in the public interest for it to succeed."
Beckett said she had considered widening the scope of the Competition Bill she plans to introduce into parliament this autumn to include reform of the merger regime.
But she added: "I intend that the current framework for considering mergers should continue, essentially unchanged, within the new Competition Commission."
Beckett said references to the new Commission should be made primarily on competition grounds.

"If the Commission finds that a merger could operate contrary to the public interest, then the decision on whether or not to block the merger and whether to permit it subject to conditions should continue to be the responsibility of ministers."
"Within this framework of impartial investigation by the Commission, I see no need to change the burden of proof in assessing the public interest," Beckett added.
The proposed new Competition Bill would introduce a prohibition based approach closely modelled on the relevant Articles of the European Union's Treaty of Rome.
Penalties of up to 10 percent of turnover would be possible where prohibitions are infringed.
"Present competition law is not working well," Beckett said. "Its reform is long overdue...We need to prevent and remedy anti-competitive behaviour more effectively."

The government has committed itself to publishing more draft bills before introducing legislation into parliament, saying it believes this will give interested parties a chance to make observations and result in better legislative proposals.
Beckett has asked for comments on this draft bill by the end of September.
